about: The code examples of the chapter 8 deck, in the order of the code slides (order = slide order). The page's chapter-code tab lists them by NAME in this order; every example is self-contained and runs with the Python standard library only; the expected result is what the run printed. The code is exactly the text of the deck's code boxes: indented per the Python standard, no prompt, no lambda.

page_requirements: Python str, bytes, list, tuple, dict and the built-ins print, len, ord, chr, enumerate, zip, max, next (no import)

examples.name: Quotes and apostrophes
examples.code:
# double quotes may hold an apostrophe
a = "Alice's cat"
# in single quotes a backslash escapes it
b = 'Bob\'s cat'
print(a, len(a))
print(b, len(b))
# b makes bytes, r still makes text
print(type(b'a').__name__, type(r'a').__name__)
examples.expected:
Alice's cat 11
Bob's cat 9
bytes str

examples.name: Escape sequences
examples.code:
# a tab and a newline are one character each
print('a\tb', len('a\tb'))
print('line1\nline2'.split('\n'))
# so are an escaped backslash and quotes
print(len('\\'), len('\''), len('\"'))

examples.name: Raw and multiline strings
examples.code:
# raw: every backslash stays as typed
path = r'C:\Users\Alice\Desktop'
print(path, len(path))
print(len(r'\n'), len('\n'))
# triple quotes hold both kinds of quote
note = '''She said "it's fine"'''
print(note)

examples.name: Index into a string
examples.code:
greeting = 'Hello, world!'
# counting starts at 0; -1 is the last character
print(greeting[0], greeting[4], greeting[-1])
# the last index is the length minus one
print(len(greeting), greeting[len(greeting) - 1])

examples.name: Slices of a string
examples.code:
greeting = 'Hello, world!'
# from start up to, but not including, stop
print(greeting[0:5], greeting[7:-1])
# leave a side empty to run to the edge
print(greeting[:5], greeting[7:], greeting[::-1])

examples.name: in, not in and immutability
concepts: The in and not in Operators
examples.code:
name = 'Zophie a cat'
# a string never changes: build a new one from slices
print(name[0:7] + 'the' + name[8:12])
# in asks whether text sits inside text
print('Hello' in 'Hello, World', 'HELLO' in 'Hello, World')
print('' in 'spam', 'cats' not in 'cats and dogs')
examples.expected:
Zophie the cat
True False
True False

examples.name: F-strings
examples.code:
name = 'Al'
age = 4000
# each brace is evaluated and pasted in
print(f'My name is {name}. I am {age} years old.')
# a sum works too; doubled braces print one brace
print(f'In ten years I will be {age + 10}. {{name}}')
examples.expected:
My name is Al. I am 4000 years old.
In ten years I will be 4010. {name}

examples.name: Format specifications
examples.code:
# after the colon: decimals, width, alignment
print(f'{3.14159:.2f}|{42:>6}|{42:^6}|')
# a comma groups thousands; #x gives hexadecimal
print(f'{1234567:,}|{255:#x}')
n = 7
# the equals sign prints the name and the value
print(f'{n=}', f'{n + 1 = }')

examples.name: Older formatting styles
examples.code:
name = 'Al'
age = 4000
# percent s slots take values in order
print('My name is %s. I am %s years old.' % (name, age))
# numbered brace slots take values by position
print('{1} years ago, {0} was born.'.format(name, age))
# neighbours join, star repeats, plus joins
print('Py' 'thon', 3 * 'un' + 'ium')
examples.expected:
My name is Al. I am 4000 years old.
4000 years ago, Al was born.
Python unununium

examples.name: Changing the case
examples.code:
s = 'Hello, world!'
# each call returns a new string; s stays as it was
print(s.upper())
print(s.lower())
# compare after lowering to ignore case
print('great' == 'GREat'.lower())
# casefold goes further: the German sharp s equals ss
print('straße'.casefold() == 'strasse')
examples.expected:
HELLO, WORLD!
hello, world!
True
True

examples.name: Testing the characters
examples.code:
# letters, a capital, letters with digits, digits, a blank
words = ['hello', 'Hello', 'abc123', '123', ' ']
# letters only, then letters or digits
print([w.isalpha() for w in words])
print([w.isalnum() for w in words])
# digits only, then blanks only
print([w.isdecimal() for w in words])
print([w.isspace() for w in words])
examples.expected:
[True, True, False, False, False]
[True, True, True, True, False]
[False, False, False, True, False]
[False, False, False, False, True]

examples.name: Testing the case
examples.code:
# digits have no case at all
words = ['hello', 'Hello', 'HELLO', 'Hello World', '123']
print([w.isupper() for w in words])
print([w.islower() for w in words])
print([w.istitle() for w in words])
examples.expected:
[False, False, True, False, False]
[True, False, False, False, False]
[False, True, False, True, False]

examples.name: Start, end and affixes
concepts: Checking the Start or End of a String
examples.code:
# test one end of the string
print('Hello, world!'.startswith('Hello'))
# a tuple accepts several endings
print('notes.txt'.endswith(('.py', '.txt')))
# cut off exactly that text, once
print('report.txt'.removesuffix('.txt'))
print('test_a.py'.removeprefix('test_'))

examples.name: Join and split
examples.code:
# join glues a list with the string between the pieces
print(', '.join(['cats', 'rats', 'bats']))
# split cuts at a chosen text, or at whitespace
print('My name is Simon'.split('m'))
print('My name is Simon'.split())
# splitlines knows every line break; partition cuts once
print('one\r\ntwo\nthree'.splitlines())
print('Monty Python'.partition(' '))
examples.expected:
cats, rats, bats
['My na', 'e is Si', 'on']
['My', 'name', 'is', 'Simon']
['one', 'two', 'three']
('Monty', ' ', 'Python')

examples.name: Justify and centre
examples.code:
# pad to a width; the bar shows the trailing padding
print('Hello'.rjust(10) + '|')
# an optional fill character replaces the spaces
print('Hello'.ljust(10, '-') + '|')
print('Hello'.center(20, '=') + '|')

examples.name: Removing whitespace
examples.code:
s = '    Hello, World    '
# the lengths show what each call cut
print(len(s), len(s.strip()), len(s.lstrip()), len(s.rstrip()))
# with an argument: any of those characters, not a word
print('SpamSpamBaconSpamEggsSpamSpam'.strip('ampS'))

examples.name: Find, count and replace
examples.code:
s = 'spam eggs spam'
# index of the first match, or -1; then count them
print(s.find('spam'), s.find('spam', 1), s.count('spam'))
# replace returns a new string; the last number limits it
print(s.replace('spam', 'ham', 1))

examples.name: Code points: ord and chr
examples.code:
# ord: character to number; chr: number to character
print(ord('A'), chr(65), chr(ord('A') + 1))
# every character has its own number
print([ord(c) for c in 'Hello'])

examples.name: Characters versus bytes
examples.code:
# four characters, but five bytes in UTF-8
print('café'.encode('utf-8'))
print(len('café'), len('café'.encode('utf-8')))
# one to four bytes per character
print([len(c.encode('utf-8')) for c in 'a€é'])
# ASCII cannot hold the accent
print('café'.encode('ascii', errors='replace'))

examples.name: The book's rjust lines, re-run
examples.code:
# count the padding Python really adds
print(len('Hello'.rjust(20)) - len('Hello'))
print(len('Hello, World'.rjust(20)) - len('Hello, World'))

examples.name: Alternating case program
Pig Latin
Table printer
examples.code:
a = ['apples', 'oranges', 'cherries', 'banana']
b = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'David']
c = ['dogs', 'cats', 'moose', 'goose']
table = [a, b, c]
# a column is as wide as its longest string
widths = []
for col in table:
    widths.append(max(len(s) for s in col))
# zip(*table) turns columns into rows
for row in zip(*table):
    cells = []
    for j, s in enumerate(row):
        cells.append(s.rjust(widths[j]))
    print(' '.join(cells))
examples.expected:
apples Alice  dogs
 oranges   Bob  cats
cherries Carol moose
  banana David goose

examples.name: Clipboard program, without the clipboard
concepts: Project 2: Add Bullets to Wiki Markup
examples.code:
# a list of one item stands in for the clipboard
shelf = ['Alice\nBob\nCarol']
# paste: read the text from the shelf
text = shelf[0]
lines = text.split('\n')
# change: a star in front of each line
starred = []
for line in lines:
    starred.append('* ' + line)
# copy: put the result back on the shelf
shelf[0] = '\n'.join(starred)
print(shelf[0])
